comments.author: @jbeezy8245
comments.text:
I love my tiny house, but I think a lot depends on how it’s built and where you live. Mine was custom built for me, so I was really specific about what I needed. I have a bathtub, washer/dryer combo, farm sink, a bigger closet, tons of built-in storage, and two mini splits because I was worried about the desert heat. It gets cold af in here 😂 and the insulation is so good I can’t even hear the train near my house.

One of my favorite things about tiny living is actually NOT having room for a bunch of junk. I don’t want to constantly consume and fill a house with stuff.

I paid around $100k for mine, put $10k down, and pay about $900 a month. I’m in Southern California and I genuinely couldn’t even rent a comparable place for $900 a month, let alone have something brand new that was built specifically for me. For $100k I might have been able to get an old fucked-up house that needed a ton of work, if I could even qualify for it.

There are definitely downsides. Tiny houses technically aren’t allowed where I live and we just don’t care 😂. I do not recommend this type of set up and thinking it's not secure but Im in an area where i can get away with it for now. I also know I probably couldn’t sell it and get all my money back, and that does suck. But I live in a rural area close enough to the city for work, so I’m lucky that the lifestyle works really well for me.

I also went with a company that had already been around since I was a teenager, so I felt pretty confident they weren’t going to build me a glorified shed and disappear.

Being a homeowner is still hard though. Apparently making the house tiny does not make the chores tiny. 😭

comments.text:
I think a large part of the problem is that tiny homes originally seemed like projects for handypeople who owned their own land or lot. They paid for materials as they were used and saved a ton of money by doing the work themselves.  This was a very affordable option for these people, who ended up owning a home outright for about 40k.  As always happens, people jumped on the bandwagon and went the tiny-home route as a solution  for the insane prices of even "moderately" priced starter homes.  They had no building experience and relied on the same developers and builders who were producing poorly built structures at inflated prices.
My boyfriend went the former route and now owns a cozy "mini" home on 5 acres for about 60k, including the land.  An electrician, he did all the wiring and much of the other finish work.  The dwelling allows for a bit of personal space, even when my boyfriend's teenaged son visits.  But it's due to the excellent design and thoughtful placement of EVERY feature of the home.  
This type of home can be a wonderful, cost-effective option, but it requires extensive planning and a lot of homework.  And in most cases a willingness to roll up one's sleeves and build some sweat equity!

comments.author: @ohiofarmer5918
comments.text:
As a builder I can tell you that you are not building a tiny house in the way you build a regular house. Normally you would have a cut room in the garage or perhaps inside a simple space within the house.
     Where are you gonna store the material? It's like working in a telephone booth and if you cut stuff outside ( maybe in the rain) it's so inefficient and drags dirt inside.
    That's why remodeling costs more than you think it should in an occupied building.
   I did buy a little 640 sq ft  house with weak floors and tired inside for 7200 forty years ago. 
   Between jobs and winter time was spent working on it and it has a nice bedroom and living room with eat in kitchen. 
   The bath was permitted but just had a toilet in a closet. I used the antique over tall doors and removed and stripped all the woodwork and made some more. I had my time and 21 thousand total in the property. 
    It's quite a nice supplement to social security and will generate revenue after I leave this veil of tears.
